Method and assumptions

Source: vignettes/method.Rmd
method.Rmd

What plan-enabled capacity is

plancap estimates plan-enabled capacity: the floor area, and the dwellings it would hold, that a district plan’s rules allow on each site. It is the answer to “what does the plan let you build here?”, site by site, summed. It is a property of the plan, not a forecast.

It is not:

  • feasible capacity: whether building it would pay at today’s prices and costs;
  • likely or realisable capacity: whether owners will sell and build;
  • infrastructure-ready capacity: whether water, wastewater and transport can serve it, unless the plan itself says so through a rule;
  • net of what is there: by default capacity is gross, on a blank slate, as if each site were empty.

These are later questions, and each starts from plan-enabled capacity.

Floor area first

Floor area is the primary output. Dwellings are a derived view: residential floor area, times an efficiency, over a dwelling size or a unit mix (conversion()), unless a zone counts dwellings by a density rule. The conversion is an assumption, stated on every summary and plot caption, not a plan rule.

Six principles

  1. Never invent a rule value. Every number carries a citation; values the plan does not state are assumptions, labelled as such.
  2. Flag, don’t drop. Every input parcel appears in every output, with a flag where it has no zone, no rules or no capacity.
  3. Floor area is primary; dwellings are derived.
  4. Gross, blank-slate capacity by default.
  5. Alternative standards are variants, built separately; each site takes the most enabling (or the one named), never a merger of the two.
  6. Unmodelled rules are registered, with the direction each would move capacity, and reported with every result.

Activity status

Plans permit some development outright and make other development subject to consent. plancap counts what a plan’s standards bound: where a plan provides for development by restricted discretionary consent and states standards for it, that development is counted, and the per-site limits of permitted activity are rules a rulebook may add (Hamilton’s vignette shows both readings as scenarios). Activities the plan discourages (non-complying, prohibited) are not counted. Every rule may record its activity_status.

What the envelope does not know

A blank-slate envelope knows the site, its boundaries and the rules. It does not know where windows, balconies, outdoor living areas, driveways and trees will go, so rules that depend on them (outlook space, separation between buildings on a site, privacy setbacks, tree canopy) are registered as not modelled, and usually make capacity an overstatement. Rules that need a layer the run does not have (a hazard map, the road hierarchy) are registered the same way until the layer is supplied.

library(plancap)
#> 
#> Attaching package: 'plancap'
#> The following object is masked from 'package:stats':
#> 
#>     density
head(unmodelled_report(rulebook_example("auckland"))[, c("rule", "likely_effect")])
#>                                                                                                             rule
#> 1                        Height in relation to boundary does not apply where a common wall exists or is proposed
#> 2                                Height in relation to boundary measured from the far side of any entrance strip
#> 3                                                Principal living room, bedroom and habitable room outlook space
#> 4                                 Outdoor living space, communal living space for developments over 20 dwellings
#> 5 Deep soil and canopy tree areas (20 m2 for sites 200-600 m2, 30 m2 for 601-1500 m2, 50 m2 for 1501 m2 or more)
#> 6     Daylight, wind, rainwater tanks, residential waste management, safety and privacy buffer, fences and walls
#>   likely_effect
#> 1   understates
#> 2   understates
#> 3    overstates
#> 4    overstates
#> 5    overstates
#> 6       unknown

Validation

plancap reproduces the capacityengine model (built for Auckland’s Unitary Plan, Christchurch and Wellington) exactly on the same inputs:

  • on an Auckland tile of 2,680 sites, every site’s floor area and dwellings match, on flat ground and with terrain, height surfaces and the front yard measured from the neighbours’ houses;
  • operative against Plan Change 120 on that tile, the change matches on every landholding (+75,092 m² of floor area, +387 dwellings).

check_capacity() reconciles every run (every parcel accounted for, land in equal to land out, floor area by storey equal to floor area by site), and check_comparison() reconciles every comparison (the drivers sum to the change; every summary reproduces both totals). The package’s tests check hand-worked cases exactly.

Units and coordinates

Rulebooks are in metres or feet (convert_rulebook_units() converts, formulas included); the engine works in metres. Parcels must be in a projected coordinate reference system.
